paragraphs: The President is to have power, "by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur." This provision has been attacked on various grounds, and often with considerable vehemence. Even so, I do not hesitate to declare my firm conviction that it is one of the best-conceived and least objectionable parts of the plan. One ground of objection is the stale topic of the intermixture of powers. Some argue that the President alone ought to have the power of making treaties; others, that it should have been placed exclusively in the Senate. Another objection arises from the small number of persons by whom a treaty may be made. Some who press this objection think the House of Representatives ought to have been brought into the business. Others seem to think it would have been enough to require two thirds of all the members of the Senate instead of two thirds of the members present. I flatter myself that the observations made in a preceding number on this part of the plan must have been enough to show it, to a discerning eye, in a very favorable light. So I shall content myself here with offering a few supplementary remarks, mainly aimed at the objections I have just stated.

On the intermixture of powers, I shall rely on the explanations already given elsewhere of the true meaning of the rule on which that objection rests. I shall take it for granted, as an inference from them, that joining the Executive with the Senate in the matter of treaties breaks no such rule. I venture to add that the particular nature of the power of making treaties shows a special propriety in that union. Several writers on government place that power among the executive authorities, but this is plainly an arbitrary classification. Look carefully at how it operates, and it will be found to have more of the legislative character than of the executive, although it does not seem to fall strictly within the definition of either. The essence of legislative authority is to enact laws, that is, to prescribe rules for regulating the society. The execution of the laws, and the use of the common strength for that purpose or for the common defense, seem to make up all the functions of the chief executive. The power of making treaties is plainly neither of these. It has nothing to do with executing the existing laws, or with enacting new ones, and still less with exerting the common strength. Its objects are CONTRACTS with foreign nations, which have the force of law but get that force from the obligations of good faith. They are not rules laid down by the sovereign for the subject, but agreements between sovereign and sovereign. The power in question therefore seems to form a distinct department, belonging properly neither to the legislative nor to the executive. The qualities I detailed elsewhere as indispensable in managing foreign negotiations point to the Executive as the fittest agent in those transactions. Yet the vast importance of the trust, and the fact that treaties operate as laws, argue strongly for the participation of the whole legislative body, or a part of it, in the business of making them.

It may be proper and safe, in governments where the chief executive is an hereditary monarch, to commit the entire power of making treaties to him. But it would be utterly unsafe and improper to entrust that power to an elected chief executive who serves four years. It has been remarked on another occasion, and the remark is unquestionably just, that an hereditary monarch, though often the oppressor of his people, has too great a personal stake in the government to be in any real danger of being corrupted by foreign powers. But consider a man raised from private life to the rank of chief executive, with a moderate or slender fortune, who looks ahead to a time not far off when he will probably have to return to the station he came from. Such a man might at times face temptations to sacrifice his duty to his interest that only exceptional virtue could resist. An avaricious man might be tempted to betray the interests of the state in order to acquire wealth. An ambitious man might make his own advancement, with the help of a foreign power, the price of his treachery to his constituents. The record of human conduct gives no warrant for so lofty an opinion of human virtue as would make it wise for a nation to commit interests as delicate and weighty as those of its dealings with the rest of the world to the sole disposal of an executive created and situated as a President of the United States would be.

Entrusting the power of making treaties to the Senate alone would have meant giving up the benefit of the President's constitutional agency in conducting foreign negotiations. True, the Senate would then be free to employ him in that role, but it would be equally free to leave him out, and pique or intrigue might lead it to choose the second course rather than the first. Besides this, the Senate's own hired agent could not be expected to enjoy the confidence and respect of foreign powers to the same degree as the constitutional representatives of the nation, and so could not act with the same weight or effectiveness. On this account the Union would lose a considerable advantage in managing its external concerns, and the people would lose the added security that would come from the Executive's cooperation. It would be imprudent to confide so important a trust to him alone, but there can be no doubt that his participation would materially add to the safety of the society. It must indeed be clear to a demonstration that the joint possession of the power in question by the President and the Senate would offer better prospects of security than possession by either of them separately. And anyone who has carefully weighed the circumstances that must come together in the appointment of a President will be satisfied that the office will always be likely to be filled by men whose character makes their concurrence in the making of treaties especially desirable, for their wisdom as well as their integrity.

The remarks made in a former number, alluded to in another part of this paper, apply with conclusive force against giving the House of Representatives a share in the making of treaties. Its membership changes constantly, and, once its future growth is taken into account, it will be a large body. We cannot expect in it the qualities essential to the proper execution of such a trust. Accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics, steady and systematic adherence to the same views, a delicate and uniform sensitivity to national character, and decision, secrecy, and dispatch are all incompatible with the character of so variable and so numerous a body. The very complication of the business, by requiring the agreement of so many different bodies, would be a solid objection in itself. The House of Representatives would have to be called on more often, and would often have to be kept together longer once assembled, in order to obtain its sanction at each stage of a treaty. That would be a source of so much trouble and expense that it alone ought to condemn the project.

The only objection left to be examined is the one that would substitute two thirds of all the members of the Senate for two thirds of the members present. It has been shown, under the second head of our inquiries, that every provision requiring more than a majority of any body for its resolutions directly tends to hamper the operations of the government and indirectly tends to subject the sense of the majority to that of the minority. This consideration seems enough to settle our opinion that the Convention has gone as far as it could in seeking the advantage of numbers in the making of treaties, consistent with the activity of the public councils and with a reasonable regard for the prevailing sense of the community. Had two thirds of the whole membership been required, then in many cases, because some members were absent, it would in practice amount to requiring unanimity. And the history of every political establishment in which this principle has prevailed is a history of impotence, perplexity, and disorder. I could offer proofs of this from the Roman Tribuneship, the Polish Diet, and the States-General of the Netherlands, if an example at home did not make foreign precedents unnecessary.

Requiring a fixed proportion of the whole body would probably do no more for the advantages of a numerous agency than merely requiring a proportion of the members attending. The former makes a fixed number necessary for every resolution, and so weakens the motives to punctual attendance. The latter makes the body's capacity to act depend on a proportion that the absence or presence of a single member can change, and so has the opposite effect. Because it promotes punctuality and so tends to keep the body complete, there is great likelihood that in this case its resolutions would generally be made by as many members as in the other, while there would be far fewer occasions of delay. It ought not to be forgotten that under the existing Confederation two members may represent a State, and usually do. Hence Congress, which now alone holds all the powers of the Union, rarely consists of more persons than would make up the intended Senate. Add to this that the members vote by States, and that when only one member from a State is present, his vote is lost. This justifies supposing that the active voices in the Senate, where the members are to vote individually, would rarely be fewer than the active voices in the existing Congress. When we also take into view the cooperation of the President, we shall not hesitate to infer that the people of America would have greater security against an improper use of the power of making treaties under the new Constitution than they now enjoy under the Confederation. And if we go one step further and look ahead to the probable enlargement of the Senate by the creation of new States, we shall not only find ample ground for confidence in the sufficiency of the members to whom that power will be entrusted, but shall probably conclude that a body more numerous than the Senate is likely to become would be very poorly fitted to discharge the trust properly.
